title: Sharing the Offerings Fairly
overview: This chapter finishes the rules for Israel's offerings, explaining who could eat which parts, when, and under what conditions.

parts.label: The guilt offering (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: This offering was for wrongs that damaged someone or broke trust, usually alongside paying back what was owed. The best fat went up in smoke on the altar, and only priests could eat the meat, inside the holy area, because it was counted as most holy.

parts.label: What the priests received (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Priests had no farmland, so they lived partly from the offerings they handled, and the priest who did the work got the meat or the animal's hide. Cooked grain offerings went to the priest on duty, while dry or uncooked ones were shared equally among all the priests.

parts.label: The thanksgiving meal (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: The fellowship offering was a shared meal where the worshipper ate most of the meat, often with family and friends, as a way of saying thank you to God. Several kinds of bread came with it, including ordinary yeast bread that was eaten at the feast rather than burned, and the meat had to be finished that same day.

parts.label: Time limits and cleanness (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Meat from a vow or a freely given offering could last two days, but on the third day leftovers had to be burned. Why is not stated, and guesses include preventing spoilage or encouraging generous sharing; eating it while ritually unclean (a temporary state from things like touching a dead animal) meant being "cut off," which scholars variously take as removal from the community or punishment left to God.

parts.label: No fat, no blood (vv. 22-27)
parts.note: The richest fat of cattle, sheep and goats was reserved for God, though fat from animals that died on their own could be put to other uses. Blood was never to be eaten because, as Leviticus explains elsewhere, it stood for the animal's life, which belonged to God.

parts.label: The priests' fixed share (vv. 28-38)
parts.note: The worshipper brought the fat and breast with their own hands, and the breast was raised toward God before going to the priests, while the right thigh went to the priest on duty. The closing lines sum up all the offering rules given in chapters 1 to 7 as coming from God at Mount Sinai.

think: Why might gratitude feel different when it is shared with others around a meal rather than kept to yourself?
